proposal.title: Guardian Reports Dispute Over Alleged NSA Wiretap in Pentagon Leak Inquiry
proposal.description_short: The Guardian reported conflicting accounts about a claimed warrantless NSA wiretap in a Pentagon leak inquiry.
proposal.description_medium: On May 27, 2025, The Guardian reported that White House advisers were told the fired aides had supposedly been identified through a warrantless NSA wiretap; the advisers said they found the claim untrue. The paper reported that Tim Parlatore denied having personally told anyone there was an illegal NSA wiretap and said information he had came from Pentagon officials. The article said the rumor’s accuracy and origin remained unclear and the episode was not formally resolved.
proposal.description_long: On May 27, 2025, The Guardian reported a dispute over a purported warrantless NSA wiretap in the Pentagon’s leak inquiry. According to the article, White House advisers were told the fired aides had supposedly been identified through such a wiretap and said they found the claim untrue. The advisers had separately been told investigators had evidence Dan Caldwell printed and photographed a top-secret document about Panama Canal military plans and sent it to a reporter. The Guardian reported that, according to the advisers, Tim Parlatore—Pete Hegseth’s lawyer overseeing the inquiry—suggested in late April that Caldwell’s phone had been wiretapped. It also says Parlatore denied having personally told anyone there was an illegal NSA wiretap and maintained he had relayed information from Pentagon officials. The article says the rumor’s accuracy and origin were unclear and that the wiretap episode was not formally resolved. It reports that the inquiry later moved to Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg’s office. This describes attributed, conflicting accounts; it does not establish that surveillance occurred or that Hegseth or Parlatore knowingly lied.
proposal.uncertainty: The report gives attributed and conflicting accounts; it says the rumor’s accuracy and origin were unclear and the wiretap episode was not formally resolved. It does not establish that surveillance occurred.

proposal.title: Trump Signed a 2025 Law Ending Some IRA Wind and Solar Tax Credits After 2027
proposal.description_short: Public Law 119-21 sets a Dec. 31, 2027 cutoff for §45Y wind/solar facilities and §48E qualified property, with a §48E storage exception.
proposal.description_medium: Public Law 119-21, signed July 4, 2025, amended the clean-electricity credits in Internal Revenue Code §§45Y and 48E. For §45Y, the law ends eligibility for applicable wind and solar facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027. For §48E, it ends the credit for qualified property at applicable wind and solar facilities placed in service after that date, while expressly excepting energy-storage technology at an applicable facility. The law does not terminate every IRA clean-energy credit.
proposal.description_long: President Donald Trump signed Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025. Sections 70512 and 70513 amend Internal Revenue Code §§45Y and 48E, the clean-electricity production and investment credits. The amended §45Y states that the credit does not apply to an “applicable facility” placed in service after December 31, 2027; for this cutoff, an applicable facility is a qualified facility using wind or solar to produce electricity. The amended §48E provides a separate cutoff: the section does not apply to qualified property placed in service after December 31, 2027 when that property is part of an applicable wind or solar facility. Section 48E expressly excepts energy-storage technology placed in service at an applicable facility from that termination paragraph. These provisions address specified wind/solar facilities and qualified property, with different statutory wording and an express storage exception; they do not state a blanket clawback of already committed funds across other clean-energy investments. Project-level eligibility must be assessed under the statute’s definitions, placed-in-service dates, and applicable transition provisions.
proposal.uncertainty: The text states statutory cutoffs and an exception, not project-level eligibility. Eligibility depends on statutory definitions, dates, and applicable transition provisions. The separate U.S. Code URL returned “Under Maintenance” and is not relied upon.
